# Analysis

Provoked by the 2026-08-10 incident landing E-1898, which produced four distinct
failures in one sitting from one underlying question: **who is allowed to define,
migrate, and use the schema, and when.**

## What governs schema writes today

`monitor.DB()` applies `schema.SQL` — all additive `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` —
on EVERY connection, plus five enum `VerifyIntegrity` gates that fail closed.
Destructive one-off change files run separately, once, at land time via
`endless db apply-change`.

E-1818 added **schema-passive**: when `dbPathOverride != ""` (set by
`PinMainDB`/`ForceRealDB`, i.e. the hook, tmux and channel surfaces) the connect
skips both the schema apply and every gate.

**The gap.** Schema-passive protects the DB from the binary. It does nothing to
protect the binary from the DB. The hook error on 2026-08-10 proves it: the
candidate binary did not migrate anything, it simply failed writing `process_id`
into a table that lacked the column. E-1818 solved one half; the unsolved half
is the one that caused the outage.

## A. What each executable does on connect

| Executable | Surface | Pins real DB? | Applies schema.sql | Runs enum gates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| global (main) | hook / tmux / channel | yes | no (passive) | no |
| global (main) | task, sql, event, ... | no | yes | yes |
| worktree (candidate) | hook / tmux / channel | yes | no (passive) | no |
| worktree (candidate) | event apply-change | no | YES | YES  <- the gate_kinds abort |
| worktree (candidate) | anything with --config-dir | no | yes (that DB) | yes |
| Python CLI | all | n/a | own bootstrap | none |

## B. Binary schema vs. DB schema

| Binary expects | DB has | Connect | Runtime DML | Observed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | main | ok | ok | normal |
| candidate | candidate | ok | ok | sandbox only |
| candidate | main | ok (passive) | FAILS: writes absent columns | hook errors, 30 min |
| main | candidate | ok (passive) | FAILS: reads dropped columns | blank board, 30 min |

Rows 3 and 4 are one defect seen from either side. NEITHER is detected at
connect; both surface as runtime SQL errors on hot paths. The enum gates cover
enum tables only and would never catch a dropped column.

## C. Landing phases

| Phase | Binary | DB | Schema | What failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 rebuild worktree bin | worktree | - | - | built from stale source (147 behind) |
| 2 backup | Python | real | pre | - |
| 3 apply-change | worktree | real | pre -> post | gate abort; later succeeded |
| 4 merge | git | - | - | FAILED -> DB post, code pre |
| 5 record landing | worktree | real | post | never reached |
| 6 just build | - | - | - | never reached; global stayed pre |

## Hypotheses to evaluate

**H1 — a migration-only executable.** Built from the landing branch, does DDL
only, never DML, so it has no runtime schema expectations to be wrong about.
Cleanly resolves phase 3. Does NOT touch table B rows 3/4, which are ordinary
binaries at runtime.

**H2 — explicit upgrade; connects verify instead of migrate.** Replace
apply-on-connect with an `endless db upgrade` verb; ordinary connects compare
the DB's schema version against the binary's and REFUSE with a clear message.
This is the one that collapses table B: rows 3 and 4 become a precise
connect-time refusal, and no binary can mutate the real ledger by opening it —
which also makes schema-passive unnecessary. Costs users an explicit step after
upgrade, and every entry point needs a good "your database needs upgrading"
message.

**Neither resolves everything, and that should be stated up front:**
- Ordering (phase 3 vs 4) is independent — see E-1941. H2 arguably makes a
  half-landed state MORE visibly broken (everything refuses) rather than less.
- Recovery is independent — see E-1942, whose shape depends on this decision:
  "copy a backup back" vs "upgrade --rollback" are different verbs.
- Whether candidate hook code should write to the real ledger at all (the
  E-998 / E-1450 tension) is a policy question this may inform but does not
  answer.

## The tension, named

E-998 points a self-dev worktree's hook at CANDIDATE code so it gets exercised.
E-1450 forces hooks to write to the REAL ledger so activity is real. Each is
correct alone; together they mean unlanded code writes production data, which
is safe exactly while the schema is unchanged and unsafe the moment it is not.

It is not a genuine catch-22. It is unresolvable only while one binary defines,
migrates, and uses the schema at once. Separating define/migrate from use — H1
and H2 together — collapses it.

## Deliverable

A decision plus the follow-on tasks it implies. Not an implementation.

# Documents on disk for external tools

## What is parked here

Only one thing: if a tool Endless has to work alongside requires markdown files
on disk in prescribed locations, Endless needs a way to keep those files current
without a human re-typing content that already lives in the ledger.

That is a generation-and-sync problem — one authoritative source rendered out to
one or more files — and nothing more. It does not need a document entity, event
kinds, section identifiers, Lexorank ordering, a proposal/review workflow, or
conflict surfacing.

## Why the original epic died

The epic was written to solve design-doc drift: ask an AI to revise a design
document and it regenerates the whole document instead of evolving the existing
one, leaving two versions that partly agree and require manual reconciliation.
The proposed fix was documents as event-sourced entities peer to tasks, with
section-level events making whole-document regeneration structurally impossible.

Brainstorm tasks solved that problem by another route. A brainstorm task is a
topic whose thinking evolves in place across sessions, in a field the tooling
already treats as authoritative, under a lifecycle that already has human review
in it. That is what the document entity was for. Once brainstorms existed, the
section-level event machinery had no problem left to solve, and every child of
this epic was obsoleted.

Two children died for reasons of their own as well. The dashboard views die with
the decision to rewrite the web surface from scratch. The ADR workflow lost to
decisions as a capability, whose storage shape is being re-decided under E-1868.

## What would revive this

A concrete external tool that reads markdown from a fixed path, where the
content it needs is already maintained in Endless. When that shows up, the tool
specifies the requirement — file layout, section conventions, refresh trigger —
far better than this placeholder can, so the right move is a fresh task written
against that tool rather than reopening the shape sketched here.

The in-repo precedent for what the mechanism would look like is the canonical
status-lifecycle mermaid block, which is duplicated byte-identically across
several documentation files and held in sync by a verification script rather
than by generation. That pattern generalizes: one source, rendered out, checked
at land time.

## Superseded design

`docs/private/endless-documents-design.md` describes the abandoned approach. It
is retained as a record of the reasoning, not as a spec. Its analysis of the
drift problem still holds; its proposed mechanism does not.

## Note on how this branch was landed

This branch could not be landed as it stood. It had been used for ten days
without ever being reset after its earlier lands, so it carried a large number
of commits whose patches were already upstream on main, plus main had moved
well ahead independently. Replaying that pile conflicted on the append-only
ledger segments — both sides had appended different lines to the same file —
once per ledger commit, so recovering and retrying could not converge.

Comparing trees rather than counting commits showed the branch was genuinely
ahead of main on exactly two files. The branch was therefore reset onto main
and those two changes re-applied, so the landing replays two clean commits
instead of the accumulated history. The discarded commits remain reachable
through the reflog from the pre-reset tip if anything is ever found missing.

The two salvaged changes are this plan itself, and the README tagline — the
newer positioning, naming AI tasks generally rather than Claude Code
specifically, which had been stranded on this branch unlanded. The tagline is
unrelated to this task's subject and rides along only because this branch is
where it was orphaned.

Why the branch went stale in the first place, and what should prevent it, is
E-1943. The narrower failure where a stale branch aborts a land on enum drift
is E-1941.

fields.title: Decide how worktree branches stop being orphaned by amended ledger commits on main
fields.description: Ledger auto-commits on main are amended in place as events append, so the tip SHA keeps changing. A worktree branch forked from one of those SHAs is orphaned from its base as soon as the next event lands: main has equivalent superset content under a new SHA, the branch points at the superseded one, and the land rebase replays the orphan and conflicts on the append-only ledger segment. E-1342's _drop_orphan_amendable_commits covers a contiguous run at the branch base only, mid-branch orphans deliberately out of scope. Decide whether to treat this as a rebase problem (widen the helper, refuse early with a named diagnosis, union merge driver, reset onto main) or as a commit-shape problem (stop amending commits other refs are forked from). See analysis.
fields.analysis:
Ledger auto-commits on main are amended in place as new events append, so the
tip commit's SHA keeps changing. A worktree branch forked from one of those
SHAs is orphaned from its base as soon as the next event lands: main holds
equivalent (superset) content under a different SHA, and the branch still
points at the superseded one. On land, the rebase replays the orphan and
conflicts on the append-only ledger segment.

`_drop_orphan_amendable_commits` (E-1342) already handles this for a
contiguous run of orphans at the branch base. Its docstring puts mid-branch
orphans out of scope deliberately: a non-amendable commit followed by an
amendable one only arose from pre-E-1309 contamination, and dropping a
mid-branch commit risks deleting intended work. The open question is what to do
when that assumption no longer holds.

Observed on the e-801 worktree. Its branch reflog showed `Created from main`
with no commits of its own before the session's, yet `git cherry main HEAD`
reported all but three of its commits as patch-equivalent to commits on main —
the inherited run of amended ledger commits. The land reported dropping base
auto-amend commits and then conflicted anyway, so the existing helper did not
cover this shape. Recovery-and-retry could not converge because each replayed
ledger commit conflicts in turn.

Two framings, and the choice between them is the point of this brainstorm.

Treat it as a rebase problem, and the levers are: widen the E-1342 helper past
contiguous-at-base once it can distinguish an inherited orphan from real work;
detect the condition before rebasing and refuse with a named diagnosis rather
than discovering it mid-conflict; give the ledger segments a union merge driver
so concurrent appends stop conflicting; or reset a branch onto main when its
base is known-orphaned and only its own commits need replaying.

Treat it as a commit-shape problem, and the lever is upstream of all of that:
amending a commit that other refs may be built on is what manufactures the
orphans. Appending a new ledger commit instead of amending would cost more
commits on main but leave every fork point stable. Whether the amend behavior
earns its keep, and what it was buying, needs establishing before the rebase-side
options are worth ranking.

Two gaps are evidence rather than separate tasks, since their fix depends on
which framing wins:

- `worktree land --dry-run` does not simulate the rebase, so it cannot predict
  the failure it exists to preview.
- `worktree drop` documents a refusal for unlanded worktrees that its
  implementation does not perform; it checks foreign state and uncommitted
  changes only. Revisit after E-1898 and E-1941 land.

Relates to E-1941, a different failure from the same root condition: `just
land` applies schema changes with a binary rebuilt from still-stale worktree
source, because the rebase onto main runs afterward.

A correction worth keeping, because it cost this session three wrong
conclusions: commit counts mislead here. A branch can read as hundreds of
commits ahead while being an ancestor of main in content. `git cherry` and a
tree comparison tell the truth; `git reflog show <branch>` tells you where the
branch actually came from, which is what finally identified the cause.

fields.title: Rework just land's ordering so no failure can leave the DB ahead of the code
fields.description: Landing E-1898 on 2026-08-10 produced two failures in the land recipe itself. First, `just land` rebuilds the worktree binary but never checks the worktree's SOURCE is current with main, so a branch 147 commits behind rebuilt a still-stale binary and aborted on an unrelated enum-drift error naming gate_kinds. Second — and the expensive one — apply-change then SUCCEEDED and the merge failed, leaving the real database migrated to a schema no installed binary understood; session tracking froze machine-wide and recovery needed a manual restore. The justfile only reasons about apply FAILING ("the land aborts before main advances"); apply succeeding and the merge failing is the unhandled, irreversible case. Fix: refuse the land when the branch is behind main, rehearse the merge on a throwaway branch, fast-forward main to that result, and apply schema changes AFTER the merge so a failed apply is merely a retry. Analysis carries the full sequence.
fields.analysis:
# Analysis

One root cause with four faces: **code and database versions diverge across the
worktree / main / real-ledger boundary, and nothing guards the seam.** All four
were hit for real on 2026-08-10, in one sitting, landing E-1898.

## Face 1 — the land uses a binary built from stale source

`just land` (justfile ~167-250) does, in order:

1. `just go` in the worktree — rebuild endless-go
2. `endless db apply-change` against the REAL DB, using that binary
3. `endless worktree land` — which rebases onto main and fast-forwards

Step 1 came from E-1709, whose comment names this failure: "A worktree rebased
onto a newer main ... but not rebuilt would land with a STALE binary whose
embedded enums no longer match the real DB's rows ... (the E-1664 guard only
checks the binary is PRESENT, not CURRENT)."

E-1709 solved half. It makes the binary match the worktree's SOURCE. Nothing
makes the source match MAIN. With the branch 147 commits behind, `just go`
faithfully rebuilt a still-stale binary and step 2 hit the same wall:

    Error: apply-change failed: open db: gate_kinds integrity check on
      ~/.config/endless/endless.db: gatekind: gate_kinds row id="2" slug="relay"
      has no matching enum constant

Nothing was wrong with gate_kinds. Main's E-1901 had added `GateKindRelay` and
applied the row; the worktree's source predated it. The rebase that would fix
this is step 3 — after the step that needs it.

## Face 2 — apply-change succeeds, the merge fails, the DB is left ahead

After rebasing by hand, the land was re-run. This time step 2 SUCCEEDED and the
land then failed, so main never got the code. Result: the real DB was migrated
to a schema only the unlanded branch understands, while every installed binary
still expected the old one. Every session query referenced a dropped column, so
all 64 sessions went unresolvable and session tracking froze machine-wide (0
writes in the following 7 minutes).

The justfile comment asserts: "If any apply fails, the land aborts before main
advances (clean recovery)." It reasons only about apply FAILING. Apply
succeeding and the merge then failing is the unhandled — and worse — case,
because it is the one that is irreversible.

## Face 3 — no supported way back (SPLIT OUT to E-1942)

`endless db backup` exists and the land calls it. There is no `endless db
restore`. Recovery was an unguided `cp`, and it went wrong twice:

- Copied over a live database with six open connections, leaving a hot
  `endless.db-journal`. A read-only connection cannot roll back a hot journal,
  so every reader returned `database is locked` and the status bar flickered.
- The backup is produced by `VACUUM INTO`, which writes a **rollback-journal**
  database. The live DB was WAL. Restoring silently changed journal mode, and
  every connection then fought over an exclusive lock to switch it back.

Recovery took: `pkill -f 'endless task show'` (four abandoned pagers holding
connections for up to 22 days), killing two `session-status --monitor`
processes, then `sqlite3 <db> 'PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; PRAGMA integrity_check;'`
to roll back the journal and restore WAL. None of that is discoverable.

A backup you cannot safely restore is not insurance.

## Face 4 — MOVED to E-1944

The worktree's Claude hook runs candidate code against the real ledger (E-998
points the hook at the candidate binary; E-1450 forces hooks to the real DB).
That pair is safe only while the schema is unchanged, and deciding it means
deciding who may define, migrate and use the schema — which is E-1944. It is
out of scope HERE so this task stays spawnable.

## Decided approach

**Face 1 — refuse, do not auto-rebase.** Before rebuilding the worktree binary,
refuse the land when `git rev-list --count HEAD..main` != 0, telling the user to
rebase. Auto-rebasing mid-land is rejected: E-1898's own rebase stopped on a
conflict in the append-only db-ledger JSONL, and a rebase that stalls with main
partly advanced is worse than a clean refusal.

**Face 2 — rehearse the merge, then reorder.** Do the merge on a throwaway
branch first (`endless-land-<taskid>-<rand>`, removed in a trap, so concurrent
lands cannot collide):

  1. branch off main, merge/rebase the task branch onto it
  2. it fails -> delete the branch, abort. The DB was never touched.
  3. it succeeds -> FAST-FORWARD main to that result. A pointer move, so there
     is no window where main advances and something else does not. Do NOT redo
     the merge; re-merging reopens the gap it just closed.
  4. THEN apply the schema changes, then record the landing, then rebuild.

Applying AFTER the fast-forward inverts the asymmetry that caused the incident:

  - apply fails after the merge -> main has the code, the DB lacks the
    migration. Re-run `endless db apply-change`; it is idempotent and gated by
    `_schema_version`. Recoverable.
  - merge fails after apply -> what happened on 2026-08-10. Not recoverable
    without a restore.

**Diagnosis, independent of the above.** Every `VerifyIntegrity` call site can
name the likely cause when the DB has rows the binary lacks: "this binary
predates the database; rebase onto main and rebuild." That direction of drift is
always staleness, never corruption. The reverse (binary has constants the DB
lacks) is a genuinely missing migration and should keep reading as it does now.

## Out of scope

E-1898 itself, which is fixed and re-verified. `endless task show -p` pinning a
DB connection for the life of its pager is a real but separate nuisance; file it
on its own if it bites again.

payload.title: Allow task update --status submitted
payload.description: endless task update --status rejects 'submitted', accepting only untriaged, unplanned, ready, underway, unverified, confirmed, assumed, completed, blocked, revisit, declined, obsolete. Every other agent-settable status can ride along with a description edit in one call; submitted cannot, so routing a task to submitted after editing its description takes a second command (task submit). That asymmetry is a direct cause of agents leaving edited tasks sitting in untriaged: the one-call path exists for 'needs a plan' but not for 'description is sufficient'. Add submitted to the accepted values; task submit stays as the standalone verb.

triage.rationale: The fix is fully specified — add 'submitted' to the accepted --status values list in task update's validation, mirroring existing agent-settable statuses.

payload.title: Fix the triager routing brainstorm tasks to unplanned
payload.description: The triager routed E-1943 (type brainstorm, description plus full analysis, no plan attached) to unplanned. For a brainstorm the plan IS the deliverable, so 'no plan attached' can never mean 'needs a plan first' — a brainstorm whose problem statement is sufficient should route to submitted and be spawnable. The triager appears to apply the same plan-attached heuristic across all task types. Make the routing type-aware: for brainstorm, judge whether the problem statement and constraints are sufficient to explore from, not whether a plan exists. Check research tasks for the same mis-read, since their deliverable is the outcome rather than a plan.

triage.rationale: The description pins down the exact fix (make triage routing type-aware, judging brainstorm/research tasks by problem-statement sufficiency rather than plan-attachment) and names the specific case to check for the same mis-read.

payload.title: Make status routing read as the agent's job at every point of occurrence
payload.description: Agents repeatedly narrate 'this sends it back through triage' after a description edit, treating the reset as a system outcome they must route around rather than a routing call they should make. Two sources teach that. CLAUDE.md documents that triage runs automatically (task add triages in the background, a sweep drains the rest), which reads as exclusivity — knowing the mechanism gives an agent nothing actionable and actively invites deferral. Reword both to lead with DECIDE YOURSELF, with the background sweep named as a worst-case fallback rather than the normal path. Drop the automation mechanics from CLAUDE.md; agents need the duty, not the machinery.

payload.title: Explore how a self-dev session reports Endless blocking it instead of working around it
payload.description: When an agent using Endless hits something that should work but does not, the reflex is to work around it silently and keep going — the user never learns the product blocked them. Observed this session: task update --status rejected submitted, and the workaround (a second task submit call) was applied without comment until asked. In self_dev mode especially, an agent is a user of the product and its friction is product signal that should surface, not be absorbed. Decide the mechanism: what counts as blocked-but-should-work versus ordinary error, how the agent surfaces it (report to the user, auto-file, a hook-collected friction log), how to avoid drowning the user in noise, and whether this applies only when self_dev is set or to any project.

triage.rationale: the description explicitly poses open design questions (blocked-vs-error criteria, surfacing mechanism, noise control, scope) without deciding among them.

payload.analysis:
`endless session status` currently renders three problems in its fault badge area, reported from a live session on 2026-08-11.

## 1. A transient fault is stuck on the badge with no visible way to resolve it

The badge shows:

```
 WARNING  1 warning — ERR-0004 job scheduling row could not be created: "triage-sufficien…
        endless errors show
```

The underlying incident is a single SQLITE_BUSY ("database is locked (5)") while creating the `triage-sufficiency` job scheduling row, first and last seen 2026-08-10T09:49:09 — one occurrence, a day stale, self-healed. By design (`internal/sessionstatuscmd/faultbadge.go`) an incident stays on the badge until `endless errors clear`, but nothing on the badge says that, so the user reads it as a permanent error with no idea how to fix it. The badge names only `endless errors show`, which explains the fault but does not offer any resolution — and `errors show` itself does not mention `errors clear` either.

Needs a decision on the fix: surface the clear command, auto-expire/auto-clear stale self-healed warnings, make single-occurrence SQLITE_BUSY on job scheduling non-faulting (it's retried anyway), or some combination.

## 2. The hint line wastes a whole screen row

`renderFaultBadge` prints a second line containing nothing but the dim string `        endless errors show`. In a status pane every row is scarce. The command hint should live on the badge line itself (right-aligned or appended) rather than consuming its own row.

## 3. The WARNING chip is unreadable

`badgeWarning = "\033[30;43m"` (black on yellow) renders as a low-contrast orange block in the user's terminal — the label is effectively invisible. Reported preference: invert the entire badge row, with a foreground/background pair that is actually readable across light and dark terminal themes.

## Files

- `internal/sessionstatuscmd/faultbadge.go` — badge rendering, colors, hint line
- `internal/sessionstatuscmd/faultbadge_test.go`
- `internal/faults/` — fault store, overview, detail log
- `internal/errorscmd/errors.go` — `errors show` / `clear` / `codes`
- `internal/jobs/run.go` — the ERR-0004 raise site

# E-1950 — session-status fault badge

Three reported defects, discussed with Mike before implementation. Decisions he
made are marked **[Mike]**.

## Defect 1 — a transient fault pinned to the badge with no way to resolve it

The incident was a single `SQLITE_BUSY` while creating the `triage-sufficiency`
job scheduling row, one occurrence, self-healed, still badged a day later.

Two independent causes:

**1a. It should never have been a fault.** `runOne` raised ERR-0004 on any
`ensureRow` failure, while `docs/errors.md` already said of that code: "no job
state is corrupted ... the next invocation retries. A persistent occurrence
means something is wrong with the database itself." Losing a single lock race is
what a database with concurrent writers does.

*Fix:* `ensureRowWithRetry` — three attempts, each behind the connection's
existing `PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000`, 250ms apart. `isBusy` matches on message
text, so a missing table or disk error still faults immediately without
retrying. **[Mike: ok]**

**1b. The dismissal was undiscoverable.** The badge named only
`endless errors show`, and `errors show` never mentioned `errors clear`. Mike
read the dim hint line as an oversight rather than an instruction.

*Fix:* `printClearHint` closes `errors show` with both forms of `errors clear`
plus the clear-is-not-retry distinction. Suppressed when nothing open.

**1c. Stale warnings age off the badge.** The E-698 design comment said clearing
is manual "so an intermittent fault cannot heal itself out of view". That rule is
right for a fault that is still happening and wrong for one that fired once and
healed. **[Mike: agreed — the existing comment contradicts his original
intention.]**

*Fix:* a warning stops being badged once **one hour of active time** has passed
since its last occurrence. Errors never age off. The incident is not cleared or
deleted — `errors show` still lists it.

**[Mike: the hour must not elapse while he is away from the computer.]** So the
clock is `monitor.ActiveSecondsSince`, which sums only the gaps between
consecutive `activity` rows shorter than `IdleGap` (5 min), plus the open segment
up to now. Idle stretches contribute nothing, so a warning cannot expire
overnight unseen. Not scoped to a project — "was the user at the machine" is not
a per-repo question.

*Placement:* the policy lives in `sessionstatuscmd`, not in `faults`. The
`faults` package deliberately imports nothing from the rest of Endless, and its
storage contract ("nothing is hidden or deleted") is unchanged — the badge simply
decides what is worth a row. `faults.Summarize` was split out of `Open` so the
filtered set produces counts consistent with what is displayed. `badgeworthy`
takes the clock as a parameter so the policy is testable without a DB.

*Failure direction:* an unreadable activity table or an unparseable timestamp
keeps the incident. Never hide what cannot be justified hiding.

## Defect 2 — the hint burned a whole screen row

`renderFaultBadge` emitted a second `Fprintln` containing only a dim
`        endless errors show`.

*Fix:* one row — chip, incident text, hint right-aligned. The hint is reserved
out of the width budget *before* the text, so it survives truncation; on a
terminal too narrow for both, the text wins and the hint is dropped rather than
wrapping.

**[Mike: `See: endless errors --help` is too long — add a shell helper `eeh` and
render it in a different background.]** So the hint is `Run eeh`, and
`eeh` joins `esu`/`esp`/`esf`/`esm` in `endless shell-init` as a wrapper for
`errors show`. The "different background" falls out of the chip inversion below.

The row fills `cols-1`, not `cols`: a line ending exactly at the right margin
sits on the deferred-wrap boundary where tmux panes can emit a spurious second
row, and the monitor sizes its pane from `frameLines`, which counts newlines and
would not see it.

**[Mike: "WARNING 1 warning" is redundant.]** Agreed — `badgeCounts` now returns
"" when there is a single incident, since the chip already says the severity. The
tally appears only when `Total >= 2`, where it says something the one chip cannot.

## Defect 3 — the WARNING chip was an unreadable orange block

Root cause: `\033[30;43m` uses the 30-47 ANSI range, which the terminal **theme
remaps**. Mike's theme renders `43` as a dark orange; black on it is invisible.
The existing code comment shows this was already tuned once in the opposite
direction for a different theme — chasing the palette cannot win.

*Fix:* fixed 256-color indices, which themes do not remap.

| | row | chip (inverts the row) |
|---|---|---|
| warning | `48;5;220` / `38;5;16` — black on gold | `48;5;16` / `38;5;220` |
| error | `48;5;160` / `38;5;231` — white on red | `48;5;231` / `38;5;160` |

**[Mike: invert the entire row — yes.]** The whole row carries the reversed
background so the badge reads as a bar; the chip inverts the row's own pair,
which delineates it without a third color that would have to be legible against
both.

## Files

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `internal/sessionstatuscmd/faultbadge.go` | rewritten: one row, 256-color inverse, stale-warning filter |
| `internal/sessionstatuscmd/session_status.go` | `frameLines` comment (badge is 1 line now, not 2) |
| `internal/monitor/activity.go` | `ActiveSecondsSince`, `IdleGap` |
| `internal/faults/read.go` | `Summarize` split out of `Open` |
| `internal/jobs/run.go` | `ensureRowWithRetry`, `isBusy` |
| `internal/errorscmd/errors.go` | `printClearHint` |
| `src/endless/cli.py` | `eeh` shell helper |
| `docs/errors.md`, `docs/guide/reference.md`, `docs/guide/orchestration.md` | retry, age-off, `eeh` |

## Verification

`esu && ./tests/tasks/e-1950-verify.sh` — 8 sections, fail-fast on the Go unit
tests, then per-defect assertions, a live render, and the docs gates.

Confirmed against Mike's real data: incident 1 (last seen 2026-08-10T09:49:09,
235 activity rows since) no longer renders on the badge, and is still open and
listed in `errors show`.

payload.text:
# Systematic backlog cull

## Why this exists

Measured over the sixty days before this task was filed: 391 tasks filed
against 264 resolved (landed plus killed). That is roughly 1.5 filed for every
one closed; over the project's life it is closer to 1.9. Any ratio above 1.0
means the backlog diverges and the project has no completion date, no matter
how fast work proceeds — working harder raises both sides of the ratio.

Near 1.0 the sensitivity is severe. Against the open count at filing time,
a sustained ratio of 0.5 clears the backlog in roughly nine months; 0.9 takes
over three years; 1.0 leaves it permanently where it is.

Filing discipline going forward is necessary but slow-acting. This task is the
fast lever: the open backlog itself.

## What to do

Sweep every open task and assign one of four dispositions. Close or park
aggressively; the bar for keeping a task open is that someone would genuinely
be worse off if it vanished.

- **obsolete** — superseded, or aimed at code or a design that no longer
  exists. Record why in the outcome, not just the status.
- **declined** — understood and deliberately not doing it. Requires a reason.
- **maybe** — plausibly wanted someday, nothing to act on now. Parking is not
  a defeat; it is what the phase is for.
- **keep** — leave open, and be able to say what makes it worth carrying.

Phase has stopped discriminating: at filing time the great majority of open
tasks sat in `now`, which makes the field carry no information. Re-phasing is
part of the sweep, not a separate pass.

## Hard constraint

**File nothing.** This task closes and parks; it does not open. A discovery
made mid-sweep belongs in an existing task's analysis, or in the report to the
user at the end — never in a new task. A sweep that files as it goes defeats
its own purpose.

Batch related tasks under one shared outcome where a group dies for one
reason; that is both faster and produces a better record than per-task prose.

## Suggested approach

Work in coherent groups rather than by ID order — by subsystem, by originating
epic, or by the design they assumed. A group that shares a premise usually
shares a fate, and judging it once is more accurate than judging its members
separately.

Prior art worth reading before starting: the sweep that obsoleted the
documents epic and the web dashboard subtree, recorded on E-801 and E-1939.
Both killed large coherent groups on a single stated premise.

## Verification

Report the before and after open counts, the split across dispositions, and
the resulting file-to-close ratio for the sweep itself. The sweep succeeds if
the open count falls materially and no new tasks were created.

Ledger auto-commits on main are amended in place as new events append, so the
tip commit's SHA keeps changing. A worktree branch forked from one of those
SHAs is orphaned from its base as soon as the next event lands: main holds
equivalent (superset) content under a different SHA, and the branch still
points at the superseded one. On land, the rebase replays the orphan and
conflicts on the append-only ledger segment.

`_drop_orphan_amendable_commits` (E-1342) already handles this for a
contiguous run of orphans at the branch base. Its docstring puts mid-branch
orphans out of scope deliberately: a non-amendable commit followed by an
amendable one only arose from pre-E-1309 contamination, and dropping a
mid-branch commit risks deleting intended work. The open question is what to do
when that assumption no longer holds.

Observed on the e-801 worktree. Its branch reflog showed `Created from main`
with no commits of its own before the session's, yet `git cherry main HEAD`
reported all but three of its commits as patch-equivalent to commits on main —
the inherited run of amended ledger commits. The land reported dropping base
auto-amend commits and then conflicted anyway, so the existing helper did not
cover this shape. Recovery-and-retry could not converge because each replayed
ledger commit conflicts in turn.

Two framings, and the choice between them is the point of this brainstorm.

Treat it as a rebase problem, and the levers are: widen the E-1342 helper past
contiguous-at-base once it can distinguish an inherited orphan from real work;
detect the condition before rebasing and refuse with a named diagnosis rather
than discovering it mid-conflict; give the ledger segments a union merge driver
so concurrent appends stop conflicting; or reset a branch onto main when its
base is known-orphaned and only its own commits need replaying.

Treat it as a commit-shape problem, and the lever is upstream of all of that:
amending a commit that other refs may be built on is what manufactures the
orphans. Appending a new ledger commit instead of amending would cost more
commits on main but leave every fork point stable. Whether the amend behavior
earns its keep, and what it was buying, needs establishing before the rebase-side
options are worth ranking.

Two gaps are evidence rather than separate tasks, since their fix depends on
which framing wins:

- `worktree land --dry-run` does not simulate the rebase, so it cannot predict
  the failure it exists to preview.
- `worktree drop` documents a refusal for unlanded worktrees that its
  implementation does not perform; it checks foreign state and uncommitted
  changes only. Revisit after E-1898 and E-1941 land.

Relates to E-1941, a different failure from the same root condition: `just
land` applies schema changes with a binary rebuilt from still-stale worktree
source, because the rebase onto main runs afterward.

A correction worth keeping, because it cost this session three wrong
conclusions: commit counts mislead here. A branch can read as hundreds of
commits ahead while being an ancestor of main in content. `git cherry` and a
tree comparison tell the truth; `git reflog show <branch>` tells you where the
branch actually came from, which is what finally identified the cause.

The orphan is not produced by amending per se. `canAmend`
(internal/events/commit.go:205-223) already refuses to amend a tip another ref
can reach — precondition 2, "HEAD must not be reachable from any ref BESIDES the
current branch." A worktree branch forked from main's ledger tip normally
triggers that refusal and endless appends instead. The commit-shape lever this
brainstorm proposes is therefore already implemented; the question is why it did
not fire.

HEAD`. `git pull --rebase` rewrites every local main commit to a new SHA. The

"contains" main's HEAD. The guard is not bypassed and does not error — it
answers a reachability question the rewrite made meaningless, returns "safe to
amend," and the next amend diverges main from every task branch.

# E-1941 — Rework `just land`'s ordering so no failure can leave the DB ahead of the code

## Context

Landing E-1898 on 2026-08-10 migrated the real database to a schema no installed
binary understood, then failed to merge. Session tracking froze machine-wide and
recovery needed a hand-rolled `cp` restore.

The cause is ordering in the dev-only `just land` recipe. It runs, in order:
rebuild the worktree binary → **`endless db apply-change` against the real DB** →
`endless worktree land` (rebase + ff-merge). The recipe's own comment reasons
only about apply *failing* ("the land aborts before main advances"). Apply
*succeeding* and the merge then failing is the unhandled case, and it is the
irreversible one.

Reproduced (`scratchpad/repro.sh` runs the real recipe body against a throwaway
repo with stubbed tools; task branch 3 commits behind main, the land stubbed to
fail as it did on 2026-08-10):

```
just go (cwd=e-9999) → endless db backup → endless db apply-change → endless worktree land ✗
DB state: MIGRATED      main advanced: NO
```

Two defects, both confirmed: there is no check that the branch is current with
main before the binary is rebuilt, and the DB is migrated before anything
irreversible is known to succeed.

**Outcome:** invert the asymmetry. Apply schema changes only after main has
actually advanced, so a failed apply is a retry rather than a restore; and
refuse the land outright when the branch is behind main, so the binary that runs
against the real DB is built from source that matches main.

## Approach

### 1. Refuse a behind-main land (justfile)

In the `land` recipe, inside the `if [ -d "$wt" ]` block and **before**
`( cd "$wt" && just go )`:

```sh
behind=$(git -C "$wt" rev-list --count HEAD..main)
if [ "$behind" -ne 0 ]; then   # refuse; tell the user to rebase
```

Refuse, do not auto-rebase — E-1898's own rebase stopped on a conflict, and a
rebase that stalls with main partly advanced is worse than a clean refusal.

This stays in the justfile and **must not** move into `endless worktree land`: a
downstream user's branch being behind main is the normal case that the land's
rebase exists to handle. Refusing there would break ordinary product usage.

### 2. Move the schema apply into `land_worktree`, after the merge

`src/endless/worktree_cmd.py`, `land_worktree()`. The apply cannot simply move
later in the justfile: Step 6 (`_record_landing`) runs the *worktree* binary
against the *real* DB, and for an enum-adding branch that binary carries a
constant the DB lacks until the change is applied — E-1664's failure inverted.
So it belongs between Step 5 and Step 6.

- **Compute the change list before Step 5**, into a local. This is load-bearing:
  after the ff-merge `main` and the branch are the same commit, so
  `git diff main...HEAD` returns empty and the changes would be silently skipped.
  Reuse the justfile's existing pathspec verbatim:
  `--diff-filter=A --name-only -- internal/schema/changes/
  ':(exclude)internal/schema/changes/runner/'`, filtered to `*.sql`/`*.go`.
- **After the ff-merge succeeds**, and only when
  `config.project_is_self_dev(main_root)`: back up, then apply each change file
  in order, pinning `endless_go_bin` (already resolved at line 2085 by
  `_resolve_land_endless_go`).
- **On apply failure**, raise a ClickException in the shape `_record_landing`
  already uses for post-merge failures (worktree_cmd.py:2001-2008): say main was
  advanced, name the cause, and state that `endless db apply-change` is
  idempotent and gated by `_schema_version` so re-running `just land` recovers.

Two new module-level helpers alongside the existing ones:
`_branch_schema_changes(worktree_path, base_branch)` and
`_apply_branch_schema_changes(paths, main_root, endless_go_bin)`.

### 3. Thread the pinned binary through `apply_change` / `backup_db`

`src/endless/event_bridge.py`. Both currently call `_resolve_endless_go()` with
no override, which is why the justfile needs its `PATH="$wt/bin:$PATH"` hack.
Add `endless_go_bin: str | None = None` to each and pass it to
`_resolve_endless_go(override=...)` — exactly the parameter `emit_event` already
threads (line 203). This finishes the job E-1664 started: it explicitly
superseded the E-1660 PATH hack for the record step, and this removes the last
one.

`cli.py`'s `db apply-change` / `db backup` commands keep their current
no-override behavior; the new parameter defaults to `None`.

### 4. Justfile cleanup

Delete the `endless db backup` call and the `for f in $changes` apply loop
(justfile:219-237) — now owned by `land_worktree`. Keep the up-front `just go`
(E-1709) and the trailing `just build`. Update the stale comment block at
justfile:193-198 whose claim "If any apply fails, the land aborts before main
advances" is the reasoning error behind the incident.

## Explicitly out of scope

**The throwaway rehearsal branch is dropped.** The analysis prescribes
rehearsing the merge on `endless-land-<tid>-<rand>`, but this needs your
sign-off to omit, because it is a deliberate departure from the written plan.
Tested in `scratchpad/exp-rebase-vs-merge.sh`: a temp branch off main with the
task branch *merged* into it conflicts on the same file, in the same cases, as
the current rebase does — PATH A and PATH B are identical in all four scenarios.
Step 4 already rebases in the worktree (main untouched, clean abort) and Step 5
is already `git merge --ff-only` (a pure pointer move), so the rehearse-then-
pointer-move shape exists. It would cost ~5 test files plus a temp-branch /
task-branch reconciliation question, and change no tested outcome.

**The `canAmend` guard and `pull.rebase` support are not fixed here.**
`scratchpad/exp-canamend-guard.sh` shows `git pull --rebase` blinds canAmend's
shared-tip guard (SHA-reachability based), which is the actual origin of the
orphaned ledger bases. That evidence is folded into E-1943's analysis, which
owns the decision. Per ED-1550 no new task was filed.

Honest limit: the behind-main refusal converts an irreversible DB-ahead disaster
into a clean refusal that says "rebase onto main" — and under a blinded guard
that rebase is the thing that conflicts. This bounds the damage; E-1943 is what
makes the land succeed.

## Files

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `justfile` (~193-237) | behind-main refusal; remove backup/apply loop; fix stale comment |
| `src/endless/worktree_cmd.py` | 2 helpers; pre-merge change list; apply between Steps 5 and 6 |
| `src/endless/event_bridge.py` | `endless_go_bin` param on `apply_change`, `backup_db` |
| `tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py` | new |
| `tests/tasks/e-1941-verify.sh` | new |

## Tests

`tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py`, following the monkeypatch style of
`tests/test_worktree_land_record_landing.py`:

- apply is invoked **after** the ff-merge and **before** `_record_landing`
  (ordering asserted via a shared call log)
- the change list is captured pre-merge and is still non-empty post-merge
- apply failure raises a re-runnable "main was advanced" error and does not
  unwind the merge
- a non-self_dev project skips apply entirely
- the pinned `endless_go_bin` reaches `_resolve_endless_go(override=...)`

## Verification

Single command: `esu && ./tests/tasks/e-1941-verify.sh`

Modeled on `tests/tasks/e-1709-verify.sh` (same pass/fail + summary shape,
exit 0/1/2), fail-fast, folding this task's own tests in:

1. **Regression, end-to-end** — the `scratchpad/repro.sh` harness promoted into
   the suite: run the real recipe body against a throwaway repo with stubbed
   `endless`/`just`, land stubbed to fail. Assert the DB was **never** migrated
   and main never advanced. This is the check that fails on today's code.
2. **Behind-main refusal** — same harness with the branch behind main: assert
   the recipe exits non-zero, names the rebase remedy, and never reaches
   `just go` or `apply-change`.
3. **Recipe ordering** (static guard, per E-1709's check 2) — `just --show land`
   contains no `endless db apply-change`, and `just go` still precedes
   `endless worktree land`. Plus `bash -n` on the recipe body.
4. **Unit tests** — `pytest tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py` and the
   existing `tests/test_worktree_land_*.py` suite.

Project-wide regression (`just test`, `just test-go`, `just build`,
`just guide-check`) I run myself and report as one line.

# E-1941 — Rework `just land`'s ordering so no failure can leave the DB ahead of the code

## Context

Landing E-1898 on 2026-08-10 migrated the real database to a schema no installed
binary understood, then failed to merge. Session tracking froze machine-wide and
recovery needed a hand-rolled `cp` restore.

The cause is ordering in the dev-only `just land` recipe. It runs, in order:
rebuild the worktree binary → **`endless db apply-change` against the real DB** →
`endless worktree land` (rebase + ff-merge). The recipe's own comment reasons
only about apply *failing* ("the land aborts before main advances"). Apply
*succeeding* and the merge then failing is the unhandled case, and it is the
irreversible one.

Reproduced by extracting the real recipe body with `just --show land` and running
it against a throwaway repo with stubbed `endless`/`just`; task branch 3 commits
behind main, the land stubbed to fail as it did on 2026-08-10 (this harness
becomes check 1 of the verify script below):

```
just go (cwd=e-9999) → endless db backup → endless db apply-change → endless worktree land ✗
DB state: MIGRATED      main advanced: NO
```

Two defects, both confirmed: there is no check that the branch is current with
main before the binary is rebuilt, and the DB is migrated before anything
irreversible is known to succeed.

**Outcome:** invert the asymmetry. Apply schema changes only after main has
actually advanced, so a failed apply is a retry rather than a restore; and
refuse the land outright when the branch is behind main, so the binary that runs
against the real DB is built from source that matches main.

## Approach

### 1. Refuse a behind-main land (justfile)

In the `land` recipe, inside the `if [ -d "$wt" ]` block and **before**
`( cd "$wt" && just go )`:

```sh
behind=$(git -C "$wt" rev-list --count HEAD..main)
if [ "$behind" -ne 0 ]; then   # refuse; tell the user to rebase
```

Refuse, do not auto-rebase — E-1898's own rebase stopped on a conflict, and a
rebase that stalls with main partly advanced is worse than a clean refusal.

This stays in the justfile and **must not** move into `endless worktree land`: a
downstream user's branch being behind main is the normal case that the land's
rebase exists to handle. Refusing there would break ordinary product usage.

### 2. Move the schema apply into `land_worktree`, after the merge

`src/endless/worktree_cmd.py`, `land_worktree()`. The apply cannot simply move
later in the justfile: Step 6 (`_record_landing`) runs the *worktree* binary
against the *real* DB, and for an enum-adding branch that binary carries a
constant the DB lacks until the change is applied — E-1664's failure inverted.
So it belongs between Step 5 and Step 6.

- **Compute the change list before Step 5**, into a local. This is load-bearing:
  after the ff-merge `main` and the branch are the same commit, so
  `git diff main...HEAD` returns empty and the changes would be silently skipped.
  Reuse the justfile's existing pathspec verbatim:
  `--diff-filter=A --name-only -- internal/schema/changes/
  ':(exclude)internal/schema/changes/runner/'`, filtered to `*.sql`/`*.go`.
- **After the ff-merge succeeds**, and only when
  `config.project_is_self_dev(main_root)`: back up, then apply each change file
  in order, pinning `endless_go_bin` (already resolved at line 2085 by
  `_resolve_land_endless_go`).
- **On apply failure**, raise a ClickException in the shape `_record_landing`
  already uses for post-merge failures (worktree_cmd.py:2001-2008): say main was
  advanced, name the cause, and state that `endless db apply-change` is
  idempotent and gated by `_schema_version` so re-running `just land` recovers.

Two new module-level helpers alongside the existing ones:
`_branch_schema_changes(worktree_path, base_branch)` and
`_apply_branch_schema_changes(paths, main_root, endless_go_bin)`.

### 3. Thread the pinned binary through `apply_change` / `backup_db`

`src/endless/event_bridge.py`. Both currently call `_resolve_endless_go()` with
no override, which is why the justfile needs its `PATH="$wt/bin:$PATH"` hack.
Add `endless_go_bin: str | None = None` to each and pass it to
`_resolve_endless_go(override=...)` — exactly the parameter `emit_event` already
threads (line 203). This finishes the job E-1664 started: it explicitly
superseded the E-1660 PATH hack for the record step, and this removes the last
one.

`cli.py`'s `db apply-change` / `db backup` commands keep their current
no-override behavior; the new parameter defaults to `None`.

### 4. Justfile cleanup

Delete the `endless db backup` call and the `for f in $changes` apply loop
(justfile:219-237) — now owned by `land_worktree`. Keep the up-front `just go`
(E-1709) and the trailing `just build`. Update the stale comment block at
justfile:193-198 whose claim "If any apply fails, the land aborts before main
advances" is the reasoning error behind the incident.

## Explicitly out of scope

**The throwaway rehearsal branch is dropped.** The analysis prescribes
rehearsing the merge on `endless-land-<tid>-<rand>`, but this needs your
sign-off to omit, because it is a deliberate departure from the written plan.
Tested across four scenarios (amend alone; `pull --rebase` alone; both; both with
a union driver) against two strategies — rebase the task branch onto main, versus
branch off main and merge the task branch in. The two gave an identical verdict
in every scenario: a temp branch with the task branch *merged* into it conflicts
on the same file, in the same cases, as the current rebase does.
Step 4 already rebases in the worktree (main untouched, clean abort) and Step 5
is already `git merge --ff-only` (a pure pointer move), so the rehearse-then-
pointer-move shape exists. It would cost ~5 test files plus a temp-branch /
task-branch reconciliation question, and change no tested outcome.

**The `canAmend` guard and `pull.rebase` support are not fixed here.**
`git pull --rebase` blinds canAmend's shared-tip guard (it is SHA-reachability
based), which is the actual origin of the orphaned ledger bases. That evidence —
the guard experiment, the struck union-merge lever, and the arguments already
tried and discarded — is folded into E-1943's analysis, which owns the decision.
Per ED-1550 no new task was filed.

Honest limit: the behind-main refusal converts an irreversible DB-ahead disaster
into a clean refusal that says "rebase onto main" — and under a blinded guard
that rebase is the thing that conflicts. This bounds the damage; E-1943 is what
makes the land succeed.

## Files

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `justfile` (~193-237) | behind-main refusal; remove backup/apply loop; fix stale comment |
| `src/endless/worktree_cmd.py` | 2 helpers; pre-merge change list; apply between Steps 5 and 6 |
| `src/endless/event_bridge.py` | `endless_go_bin` param on `apply_change`, `backup_db` |
| `tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py` | new |
| `tests/tasks/e-1941-verify.sh` | new |

## Tests

`tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py`, following the monkeypatch style of
`tests/test_worktree_land_record_landing.py`:

- apply is invoked **after** the ff-merge and **before** `_record_landing`
  (ordering asserted via a shared call log)
- the change list is captured pre-merge and is still non-empty post-merge
- apply failure raises a re-runnable "main was advanced" error and does not
  unwind the merge
- a non-self_dev project skips apply entirely
- the pinned `endless_go_bin` reaches `_resolve_endless_go(override=...)`

## Verification

Modeled on `tests/tasks/e-1709-verify.sh` (same pass/fail + summary shape,
exit 0/1/2), fail-fast, folding this task's own tests in:

1. **Regression, end-to-end** — the reproduction harness from Context, promoted
   into the suite: extract the recipe body with `just --show land`, run it against
   a throwaway repo with stubbed `endless`/`just`, land stubbed to fail. Assert
   the DB was **never** migrated and main never advanced. This is the check that
   fails on today's code.
2. **Behind-main refusal** — same harness with the branch behind main: assert
   the recipe exits non-zero, names the rebase remedy, and never reaches
   `just go` or `apply-change`.
3. **Recipe ordering** (static guard, per E-1709's check 2) — `just --show land`

   `endless worktree land`. Plus `bash -n` on the recipe body.
4. **Unit tests** — `pytest tests/test_worktree_land_schema_apply.py` and the
   existing `tests/test_worktree_land_*.py` suite.

Project-wide regression (`just test`, `just test-go`, `just build`,
`just guide-check`) I run myself and report as one line.

# Analysis

Provoked by the 2026-08-10 incident landing E-1898, which produced four distinct
failures in one sitting from one underlying question: **who is allowed to define,
migrate, and use the schema, and when.**

## What governs schema writes today

`monitor.DB()` applies `schema.SQL` — all additive `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` —
on EVERY connection, plus five enum `VerifyIntegrity` gates that fail closed.
Destructive one-off change files run separately, once, at land time via
`endless db apply-change`.

E-1818 added **schema-passive**: when `dbPathOverride != ""` (set by
`PinMainDB`/`ForceRealDB`, i.e. the hook, tmux and channel surfaces) the connect
skips both the schema apply and every gate.

**The gap.** Schema-passive protects the DB from the binary. It does nothing to
protect the binary from the DB. The hook error on 2026-08-10 proves it: the
candidate binary did not migrate anything, it simply failed writing `process_id`
into a table that lacked the column. E-1818 solved one half; the unsolved half
is the one that caused the outage.

## A. What each executable does on connect

| Executable | Surface | Pins real DB? | Applies schema.sql | Runs enum gates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| global (main) | hook / tmux / channel | yes | no (passive) | no |
| global (main) | task, sql, event, ... | no | yes | yes |
| worktree (candidate) | hook / tmux / channel | yes | no (passive) | no |
| worktree (candidate) | event apply-change | no | YES | YES  <- the gate_kinds abort |
| worktree (candidate) | anything with --config-dir | no | yes (that DB) | yes |
| Python CLI | all | n/a | own bootstrap | none |

## B. Binary schema vs. DB schema

| Binary expects | DB has | Connect | Runtime DML | Observed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | main | ok | ok | normal |
| candidate | candidate | ok | ok | sandbox only |
| candidate | main | ok (passive) | FAILS: writes absent columns | hook errors, 30 min |
| main | candidate | ok (passive) | FAILS: reads dropped columns | blank board, 30 min |

Rows 3 and 4 are one defect seen from either side. NEITHER is detected at
connect; both surface as runtime SQL errors on hot paths. The enum gates cover
enum tables only and would never catch a dropped column.

## C. Landing phases

| Phase | Binary | DB | Schema | What failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 rebuild worktree bin | worktree | - | - | built from stale source (147 behind) |
| 2 backup | Python | real | pre | - |
| 3 apply-change | worktree | real | pre -> post | gate abort; later succeeded |
| 4 merge | git | - | - | FAILED -> DB post, code pre |
| 5 record landing | worktree | real | post | never reached |
| 6 just build | - | - | - | never reached; global stayed pre |

## Hypotheses to evaluate

**H1 — a migration-only executable.** Built from the landing branch, does DDL
only, never DML, so it has no runtime schema expectations to be wrong about.
Cleanly resolves phase 3. Does NOT touch table B rows 3/4, which are ordinary
binaries at runtime.

**H2 — explicit upgrade; connects verify instead of migrate.** Replace
apply-on-connect with an `endless db upgrade` verb; ordinary connects compare
the DB's schema version against the binary's and REFUSE with a clear message.
This is the one that collapses table B: rows 3 and 4 become a precise
connect-time refusal, and no binary can mutate the real ledger by opening it —
which also makes schema-passive unnecessary. Costs users an explicit step after
upgrade, and every entry point needs a good "your database needs upgrading"
message.

**Neither resolves everything, and that should be stated up front:**
- Ordering (phase 3 vs 4) is independent — see E-1941. H2 arguably makes a
  half-landed state MORE visibly broken (everything refuses) rather than less.
- Recovery is independent — see E-1942, whose shape depends on this decision:
  "copy a backup back" vs "upgrade --rollback" are different verbs.
- Whether candidate hook code should write to the real ledger at all (the
  E-998 / E-1450 tension) is a policy question this may inform but does not
  answer.

## The tension, named

E-998 points a self-dev worktree's hook at CANDIDATE code so it gets exercised.
E-1450 forces hooks to write to the REAL ledger so activity is real. Each is
correct alone; together they mean unlanded code writes production data, which
is safe exactly while the schema is unchanged and unsafe the moment it is not.

It is not a genuine catch-22. It is unresolvable only while one binary defines,
migrates, and uses the schema at once. Separating define/migrate from use — H1
and H2 together — collapses it.

## Deliverable

A decision plus the follow-on tasks it implies. Not an implementation.



## Folded in from E-1922: the concrete form of H2

E-1922 was filed separately as an implementation of exactly H2's connect-time
check, and is folded here because it presupposes a decision this task has not
yet made. Its evidence stands regardless of which hypothesis wins, and is worth
keeping in front of whoever decides:

`monitor.DB()` executes its embedded schema SQL on every owned connection with
no check that the DB carries the change files that schema assumes. Nothing
connects a binary's expectations to the DB's actual state, so a binary
installed before its change file is applied can create schema objects
referencing columns that do not exist. E-1917's trigger reads
`NEW.changed_by_session`, and SQLite resolves trigger bodies at fire time, so
every `UPDATE tasks` would fail — the failure is not at connect, it is at the
next write, which is what makes it hard to attribute.

Today that is avoided only by convention: land, which runs apply-change, before
`just install`. A convention is not a guard, and the ordering requirement is
invisible to anyone who has not been bitten by it.

E-1922 proposed a gate that either auto-applies pending changes on connect or
refuses with a clear error. Note that those are two different answers, not one:
auto-applying keeps a binary able to migrate whatever DB it opens, which is the
property H1 and H2 are both trying to remove; refusing is H2 proper. If H2 is
chosen, this becomes its first follow-on task. If H1 is chosen instead, the
convention-only ordering requirement still needs an answer, and this evidence
is where that answer starts.

payload.outcome: Folded into E-1944, whose analysis now carries this evidence. E-1922 implemented one of E-1944's two hypotheses (replace apply-on-connect with a connect-time schema-version check that refuses rather than silently fixing) before E-1944 had decided between them. E-1944 states its deliverable is a decision plus the follow-on tasks it implies, so this re-emerges as a follow-on if that hypothesis wins, and is obsolete if the migration-only-executable hypothesis wins instead. The underlying evidence — monitor.DB() applying schema on every connection with nothing tying a binary's expectations to the DB's state, and the ordering requirement being convention rather than a guard — survives either way and is preserved there.

fields.title: Decide how worktree branches survive a rewrite of main's history

fields.description: Worktree branches lose their base when main's history is rewritten under them — not from amending. canAmend already refuses to amend a tip another ref can reach, but implements that as SHA reachability, so once `git pull --rebase` rewrites main the guard answers a question the rewrite made meaningless, permits the amend, and the land rebase then conflicts on the append-only ledger segment. Endless must work under either `pull.rebase` setting: rebase-style pull is mainstream, and a guard that silently degrades under it is a defect regardless of which setting this repo uses. Decide how — give a fork point an identity that survives a rewrite, keep rewrites away from ledger commits, or detect the condition before rebasing and refuse with a named diagnosis. Any SHA-reachability-based fix inherits the same blindness; the union-merge-driver option is struck (it would corrupt the ledger). Analysis carries the evidence. Deliverable is a decision plus follow-on tasks.

payload.analysis:
`task report` models a report as a one-shot render with no partial success and
no persisted state, so any rejected or absent field costs a full extra
invocation. One task rather than four: the symptoms below share that cause.

Evidence — one turn of an E-1939 session took three calls to emit one block:

1. ALL-OR-NOTHING VALIDATION. A payload of {verify, notes} had its note bounced
   by the ceremony check, and the command emitted NO block at all — the valid
   `verify` field was discarded alongside the rejected note. Rendering the block
   from the accepted fields, plus a rejection notice naming what was dropped and
   why, would have made this the last call instead of the middle one.

   The check's judgment was CORRECT: the note recounted a rebase and its
   conflict resolution, which a reviewer can read off the commits. The defect is
   the blast radius of a rejection, not the rejection itself.

2. STATELESSNESS IS UNDISCOVERABLE. The command is addressed by task id, takes a
   structured payload, and sits beside `task update` / `task submit`, which
   persist. It does not persist — a payload supplied in one call is gone by the
   next. The session spent a call running it bare to find that out. Either
   persist the payload on the task, or make the one-shot nature evident in the
   help text and the `--json` option description.

3. AN EMPTY BLOCK AT `unverified` IS NEAR-CERTAINLY WRONG. Run bare on a task
   just flipped to `unverified`, it prints `Nothing to report.` — for a task
   whose handoff mandates a verify command. It cannot know that command, but it
   does know the status and that no `verify` entry was passed, so it can say so
   rather than assert a null result the handoff forbids.

4. THE PostToolUse HOOK FIRES ON `--help`. Running `task report --help` to look
   up the `--json` shape injects the full "now append the block, unchanged,
   after the separator" instruction when no block was rendered. The hook matches
   the command name rather than a successful render.

Deliberately out of scope: the ceremony check's judgment criteria. They are
working, and loosening them to reduce round-trips would trade a real quality
gate for a cheap one.
